analysis.title: Global Economics Wrap-Up: October 29, 2026
key_insights: Global growth has been 'remarkably unremarkable' this year: fiscal easing and the AI boom roughly offset the drag from the Iran war and lingering US tariffs. Oil price risks remain skewed to the upside.

DM yield curves have risen by about 100bp on average since early 2026. GS estimates this would subtract a cumulative 0.6% from GDP through weakness in housing, consumer durables and business investment if sustained.
GS says the peak impulse from the AI boom is passing. It expects AI investment as a share of US GDP and the boost to US consumer spending from asset appreciation to diminish in coming quarters.

AI labor market effects are showing up beyond the technology sector. Adoption is positively correlated with unemployment and negatively correlated with payrolls growth across non-manufacturing industries.
GS expects significant disinflation progress next year but still expects another 25bp FOMC hike in December, then renewed cuts in late 2027/early 2028.
Tighter financial conditions are likely to weigh on Euro area growth. UK growth forecasts have drifted higher after upside GDP surprises this year.

Slightly faster Chinese Q3 growth lifted GS's 2026 China forecast to 4.6%, but most activity indicators point to weak domestic demand. Sustained growth in the 4.5-5% target range would require steep increases in the trade surplus, already at 1% of global GDP.
The FOMC voted 10-2 to hold the fed funds rate at 3.75-4%, in line with GS and consensus. Fed officials have pointed to a compromise of hiking every other meeting.
The BoC raised its policy rate 25bp to 2.5% and stressed rising cost pressures. GS expects a hold in December and a final 25bp hike in January.
The ECB held its policy rate at 2.5%, in line with expectations. ECB President Christine Lagarde announced her resignation, effective February 7.
The RBNZ surprised by keeping the OCR at 2.75% in a split 4-3 decision. GS expects 25bp hikes in December (to 3.00%) and March (to 3.25%), well below market pricing.
Direct inflation pressure from the AI buildout is limited in most economies (about 0.1pp) because categories exposed to memory prices carry smaller weights outside US core PCE.

GS estimates a yoy core inflation boost of about 19bp in 2027Q1 in non-US DMs, versus a peak of 50bp for US core PCE and 20bp for US core CPI. The overall boost is 0.2-0.3pp in non-US DMs, 0.6pp for US core PCE, 0.3pp for Japan and 0.2pp for the UK, and it should fade through 2027 as memory price pressures diminish.
Indirect inflation effects via higher activity look small: a moderate 0.3% GDP boost and less than 0.1pp inflation boost in DMs on average through end-2026.

GS expects a second and final Fed hike in December, with a third in March possible if inflation runs higher than expected. It read Chairman Warsh's comments as balanced and consistent with a slower pace and a limited total number of hikes.
US Q3 real GDP grew 3.4% annualized. Consumer spending rose 3.8% and business fixed investment rose 12.7%, mostly AI-related equipment, while housing investment fell 3.4%.
GS launched its US Q4 GDP tracking estimate at +1.8% annualized: business fixed investment +8.2%, consumer spending +1.8% as fiscal stimulus fades, and residential investment -5.0%.
UK Autumn Budget broadly matched expectations. The deficit was revised up by about £13bn per year on average and headroom against the deficit rule fell to £15bn from £24bn, in line with consensus.

GS expects Euro area October headline HICP at 3.88% yoy and core at 2.53%, with services at 3.21% and core goods at 1.29%. Its Q3 Euro area GDP tracking estimate rose to +0.42% qoq from +0.21% because of an Irish upside surprise, and is about +0.21% excluding Ireland.

Euro area fiscal policy has been a growth tailwind this year but turns broadly neutral next year. GS expects the EMU4 deficit to widen to 4.0% of GDP in 2026 and 4.2% in 2027, with fiscal policy adding 0.1pp to 2026 growth.

Brazil: Lula won a fourth term with 51.8% of valid votes, but conservatives did well in gubernatorial and congressional races. Fiscal policy is the market focus, with deficits above 8% of GDP and public debt above 82% of GDP.
EM central banks: Chile held at 4.5%, Turkey cut 100bp to 36% and restarted easing, Russia held at 14% and signaled higher for longer, Kazakhstan cut 50bp to 15.75%, and Thailand held at 1%.

Strong composition: consumer spending +3.8%, business fixed investment +12.7%, housing investment -3.4%.
GS expects slower consumer spending as fiscal stimulus fades, with AI-driven investment still strong.
GS expects inflation to rise further in October.
Services inflation expected at 3.21% and core goods at 1.29%.
Above consensus, driven by Ireland. About +0.21% excluding Ireland.
A 25bp hike with emphasis on rising cost pressures. GS expects a hold in December and a final hike in January.
Unchanged in a split 4-3 decision, a surprise. GS expects hikes to 3.00% in December and 3.25% in March.
Raised on slightly faster Q3 growth, but domestic demand remains weak.
A 100bp cut restarted the easing cycle.
Held as expected, with a signal of higher rates for longer.
A 50bp cut. GS expects 15.25% by year-end.

risk_factors: Oil price risks skewed to the upside, hurting consumers and energy-importing economies.
DM yield curves up about 100bp since early 2026 could subtract a cumulative 0.6% from GDP if sustained.
The AI boom impulse to US investment and consumer wealth effects is fading.
AI adoption is raising unemployment and lowering payrolls growth in non-manufacturing industries.
Higher inflation could prompt a third Fed hike in March.
Chinese growth in the target range requires a steep rise in the trade surplus, already 1% of global GDP.
Brazil's fiscal deficit above 8% of GDP and debt above 82% of GDP, with a more conservative Congress limiting reform.
Tighter financial conditions weigh on Euro area growth, and the fiscal tailwind fades next year.
geopolitical: The Iran war is a negative impulse to global growth, and oil price risks remain skewed to the upside.
Lingering US tariffs continue to drag on global growth.
Brazil's President Lula won reelection with 51.8% of valid votes, while conservatives performed strongly in congressional and gubernatorial races.
ECB President Christine Lagarde announced her resignation, effective February 7.
UK Autumn Budget raised taxes slightly and funded the Defence Investment Plan.

tension_points.bull_case: GS reads Chairman Warsh's comments as balanced and consistent with a slower every-other-meeting pace and a limited total number of hikes, with significant disinflation expected next year.
tension_points.bear_case: A third hike in March is possible if inflation comes in higher than GS expects, and the AI buildout adds to core inflation through memory prices.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Inflation coming in higher than GS expects, which would bring a third hike in March.

theme_stances.key_argument: Fed officials point to a compromise to hike every other meeting, and this week's meeting gave little reason to deviate, so a second and final hike is expected in December.
theme_stances.evidence: compromise to hike every other meeting

theme_stances.key_argument: Direct and indirect inflation pressure from AI demand is limited outside US core PCE and should fade through 2027 as memory price pressures diminish.
Higher yields, upside oil risks and a fading AI impulse argue for downside risks to global growth.
theme_stances.evidence: Global growth has been remarkably unremarkable this year
